title: What time is it?
goal: Tell the time in Dutch — including *half*, which points forward, not back — name days and months, and make appointments.
bekal: read an analog clock with *over*, *voor*, *kwart* and *half*
wave: Review **Unit 6**: say ten random prices out loud in Dutch, then write down the figures and check yourself.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Een afspraak maken
dialogs.intro: Budi phones the dentist. He thinks he has numbers down. He's wrong.

lines.speaker: Assistent:
lines.id: De Vries dental practice, good morning.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Goedemorgen, u spreekt met Budi Santoso. Ik wil graag een afspraak maken.
lines.id: Good morning, this is Budi Santoso. I'd like to make an appointment.
lines.literal: good-morning, you speak with Budi Santoso. I want gladly an appointment make.

lines.speaker: Assistent:
lines.text: Dat kan. Kunt u donderdag om half drie?
lines.id: Certainly. Can you make Thursday at half past two?
lines.literal: that can. can you Thursday at half three?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Half drie… so half past three?

lines.speaker: Assistent:
lines.text: Nee hoor. Half drie is twee uur dertig.
lines.literal: no really. half three is two hour thirty.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ah — een half uur vóór drie, niet erna.
lines.id: Ah — half an hour before three, not after.
lines.literal: ah — a half hour before three, not there-after.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Donderdag half drie is prima. Hoe laat moet ik er zijn?
lines.id: Thursday at half past two is fine. What time should I be there?
lines.literal: Thursday half three is fine. how late must I there be?

lines.speaker: Assistent:
lines.text: Vijf minuten van tevoren. En neem uw verzekeringspas mee.
lines.id: Five minutes early. And bring your insurance card.
lines.literal: five minutes from before. and take your insurance-card along.

lines.speaker: Assistent:
lines.id: See you Thursday. Have a nice day!

notes: **U spreekt met …** is the standard way to introduce yourself on the phone — not *ik ben*. Literally "you are speaking with …".

**Half drie = 2:30.** This is the most famous time trap in Dutch, and it really does make people show up an hour off. Dutch (like German) counts *half* towards the **next** hour: *half drie* = halfway to three o'clock. English "half three" (British for 3:30) means the opposite — forget it here.
**Kunt u donderdag om half drie?** — the verb *komen* is dropped because it's obvious. The full sentence: *Kunt u donderdag om half drie komen?*

**Iedereen struikelt daarover** — *daarover* = "over that" (literally "thereover"). *Daar* + a preposition replaces "that" for things and ideas, like old English *therefore*, *thereby*. You'll meet *daarom*, *daarmee*, *daarnaast* all the time.
**Van tevoren** = beforehand, in advance. For appointments in the Netherlands, being on time means arriving **five minutes early**; ten minutes late already counts as rude and can cost you your slot.

**Neem uw pas mee** — *meenemen* (to take along) is a separable verb: its first part (*mee*) gets thrown to the end of the sentence, like English "bring it *along*". The whole family is covered in the next unit.
**Doe ik** — a super-short answer meaning "I will". The full form is *dat doe ik*.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: Dutch divides every hour into four reference points: the full hour, quarter past, half, and quarter to. Every other minute is counted from the nearest point.
after: Look at the rows from 14:20 to 14:40: Dutch **counts from the half hour**, not from the full hour. *Tien voor half drie* isn't "ten to three" but "ten before 2:30" = 2:20. It takes practice, but once it sticks it actually feels more precise.

To avoid misunderstandings, the Dutch themselves often use the digital form: *twee uur dertig*, *veertien uur dertig*. At stations, airports and on official schedules the 24-hour clock is **always** used.
The questions: *Hoe laat is het?* (literally: "how late is it?") and *Hoe laat begint het?* To give the time of an appointment, use the preposition **om**: *om half drie*, *om acht uur*.

grammars.title: Days, months and parts of the day
body: Days and months are written in **lowercase** — unlike English.
after: Days take the preposition **op**: *op maandag*, *op zondag* (on Monday, on Sunday) — but in speech the preposition is often dropped: *Ik werk maandag.*

Parts of the day: *de ochtend* (morning), *de middag* (afternoon), *de avond* (evening), *de nacht* (night). For habits, use the **'s** form: *'s ochtends*, *'s middags*, *'s avonds*, *'s nachts* — "in the mornings", "at night".
Dates use ordinary numbers: *op 5 mei* is read *op vijf mei*. For the 1st, use *één* or *de eerste*: *de eerste januari*.

head: Nederlands
English
rows: Ik wil graag een afspraak maken.
I'd like to make an appointment.
Kunt u dinsdag om tien uur?
Can you make Tuesday at ten?
I need to reschedule the appointment.

blocks.title: The agenda: a Dutch habit you must understand
items: Almost everything in the Netherlands is **arranged in advance** — even visiting friends. Dropping by unannounced comes across as startling, not warm.
*Even in mijn agenda kijken* ("hang on, let me check my calendar") is a sentence you'll hear every time you invite someone.
A dinner date can be set three weeks ahead, and that's normal.
If you have to cancel, say so as early as possible: *Sorry, ik moet onze afspraak afzeggen.* Canceling on the day without a good reason leaves a bad impression.
⚠️ Doctors, dentists and government offices charge a fee if you don't show up without canceling (*no-show*).

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Morgen* means **tomorrow**, while *ochtend* means morning — yet *vanmorgen* means "this morning" and *goedemorgen* means "good morning". One word, two lives (just like old English *morrow* and *morning*); the compound decides which.

Time words very often stand **at the start of the sentence** in Dutch, and as soon as one does, the verb jumps to second place: *Morgen **ga** ik naar Amsterdam.* This is exactly the rule taken apart in Unit 10.

items: I'd like to make an appointment.
Can you make Thursday at half past two?
